source_first_seen.unit_name: Why reinforcement learning is needed
source_first_seen.unit_summary: Deep reinforcement learning is framed as the combination of deep learning with reinforcement learning, with RLHF previewed as a later application for aligning language models [ts=57s] [ts=121s]. The Go example shows why classic supervised learning from professional moves is limited: the data cannot cover the state space, may copy suboptimal human moves, and lacks the player's long-term strategy [ts=639s] [ts=842s]. RL is summarized as automatically learning good sequences of decisions and as teaching by experience rather than by examples [ts=649s] [ts=677s]. The agent-environment loop defines actions, states, observations, rewards, and transitions, with partial observability illustrated by fog-of-war games where observation contains less information than the true state [ts=867s] [ts=977s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Exposure bias, alternative training schemes, and RLHF context
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The lecture revisits repetition from the training side and argues that maximum-likelihood language models can assign high probability to bad degenerate strings [ts=2473s]. The core diagnosis is exposure bias: under teacher forcing the model trains on gold prefixes, but at generation time it must condition on its own imperfect outputs, creating a harmful train-test mismatch [ts=2510s] [ts=2541s]. Scheduled sampling narrows this gap by mixing model-generated and gold tokens with a probability that increases through training, though the objective can be unstable [ts=2560s]. DAgger similarly augments training data with model-generated sequences so the model learns on states it will actually encounter [ts=2603s]. The lecture also presents retrieval-augmented generation, where the model begins from a retrieved prototype and edits it by insertion, deletion, or swapping, reducing exposure bias because generation no longer starts from scratch left-to-right [ts=2655s]. Reinforcement learning is then framed as an MDP over states, actions, policies, and rewards, with rewards derived from automatic metrics or human preference [ts=2693s] [ts=2827s]. The lecture warns that optimizing BLEU or ROUGE can game the metric rather than improve true quality [ts=2744s]. It finishes with the modern pipeline behind ChatGPT-style systems: large-scale pretraining, instruction tuning, and then RLHF, with RLHF viewed as difficult from scratch but effective on top of a strong pretrained model [ts=3110s] [ts=3130s].

source_first_seen.unit_name: Tabular reinforcement learning with the recycling example
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The recycling example defines a five-state environment with terminal states, left/right actions, and rewards for throwing garbage away, picking up packaging, and reaching a recycle bin [ts=1081s] [ts=1156s]. Long-term return is introduced as a discounted sum of rewards, with gamma between 0 and 1 encoding how much future reward is devalued [ts=1261s] [ts=1325s]. A Q-table is defined as a states-by-actions matrix whose entries estimate how good it is to take an action in a state, which would solve the decision problem if known [ts=1452s] [ts=1499s]. Backtracking through immediate rewards produces discounted returns in the toy tree, and the Bellman optimality equation formalizes that an optimal Q value equals immediate reward plus discounted best future Q value [ts=1642s] [ts=1871s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Deep Q-learning and bootstrapped targets
target_first_seen.unit_summary: Deep Q-learning replaces a memory-heavy Q-table with a neural Q-function, using a forward pass to estimate action values from a state [ts=2136s] [ts=2161s]. For the toy example, a one-hot encoded state is fed to a network whose output layer has one Q-value per action; more actions would require more output neurons [ts=2187s] [ts=2216s]. The training target is bootstrapped from immediate reward plus discounted maximum Q-value at the next state, while that target is held fixed for the current backpropagation step [ts=2476s] [ts=2524s]. The vanilla DQN loop initializes the Q-network, loops through episodes and time steps, selects the action with maximum Q-value, observes reward and next state, computes the target/loss, and updates parameters with gradient descent [ts=3107s] [ts=3163s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: The DQN target and regression loss are direct neural approximations of the Bellman optimality backup.

p5_trace.keep_rationale: DQN targets and loss are bootstrapped from the Bellman optimality equation.

source_first_seen.unit_name: From long recordings to windowed labels
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The proposed labeling scheme turns each long recording into multiple short windows and marks a window positive only when it ends right after the speaker finishes "Robert, turn on" [ts=1661s] [ts=1776s]. This turns roughly 100 long clips into around 3,000 binary examples, which is operationally convenient for training a classifier [ts=1775s] [ts=1798s]. The first model then reports 97% accuracy while producing zero detections, revealing that the dataset is so skewed that always predicting the negative class looks strong under the naive metric [ts=1813s] [ts=1860s]. The segment uses this to motivate rebalancing strategies rather than trusting headline accuracy alone [ts=1914s] [ts=1978s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Balancing data, fighting overfitting, and building robustness
target_first_seen.unit_summary: After the imbalance fix, the next observed failure is a train/dev gap: the model does well on train but only about 50% on the dev set, which the lecture interprets as overfitting and a cue to try regularization or more data [ts=2260s] [ts=2411s]. The instructor then describes a synthetic augmentation trick that works in speech: add clean trigger utterances to background-noise recordings so the summed waveform simulates speech in realistic environments [ts=2495s] [ts=2583s]. He warns that using only trigger phrases would teach voice activity detection rather than phrase recognition, so negative examples must also include other spoken content [ts=2608s] [ts=2664s]. The segment closes with a rule of thumb that richer and more diverse training data usually wins, provided the model has enough capacity to absorb that diversity [ts=2803s] [ts=2858s].

source_first_seen.unit_summary: The lecture frames the session as a practical tour of techniques for building LLM applications beyond the base model, including prompting, RAG, agentic workflows, evals, and multi-agent systems [ts=5s]. Students identify base-model limitations such as missing domain knowledge, distribution shift, lack of current information, and poor fit for narrow enterprise tasks [ts=228s]. The instructor adds control failures, style/format inconsistency, task-specific understanding, limited context windows, and source requirements as recurring reasons a vanilla LLM underperforms [ts=475s]. RAG is previewed as a way to retrieve compressed document representations and attach relevant evidence to the prompt, but the lecture also notes latency and future-proofing debates [ts=856s]. target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 7: Beyond the Model: Enhancing LLM Applications
target_first_seen.unit_name: RAG pipeline and common retrieval improvements
target_first_seen.unit_summary: RAG is introduced as a response to standalone LLM problems: limited context, difficulty finding facts in long contexts, knowledge cutoffs, hallucinations, and lack of sources [ts=2709s]. The core idea is to integrate external knowledge sources such as databases, documents, or APIs so answers can be more accurate, up to date, grounded, and developer-controllable without retraining the model [ts=2783s]. In the medical QA example, documents are embedded into lower-dimensional representations, stored in a vector database, and retrieved by comparing the embedded user query against document embeddings [ts=2831s]. The retrieved documents are added to the prompt with instructions such as answering only from the documents and saying "I don't know" when the answer is absent [ts=2955s]. The unit then covers chunking for large documents and HyDE, where the query is first expanded into a hypothetical document whose embedding may be closer to target documents [ts=3049s].

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 3: Full Cycle of a Deep Learning Project
source_first_seen.unit_name: Data quality, distribution mismatch, and model capacity
source_first_seen.unit_summary: Data quality matters because low-quality examples, such as blurry face images, can be less useful than sharp in-focus examples when they do not match the desired recognition setting [ts=1925s]. The instructor then addresses distribution mismatch: training data should be relevant, but it does not always need to come from exactly the same distribution as the test set [ts=1981s]. Larger neural networks can often absorb somewhat irrelevant but non-incorrect data without hurting the core task as much as smaller models would [ts=2034s]. This section bridges data choices to deployment by returning to the trained face-recognition model as software that must run inference in a real system [ts=2211s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 3: Full Cycle of a Deep Learning Project
target_first_seen.unit_name: Benchmarks, drift, monitoring, and maintenance after deployment
target_first_seen.unit_summary: For model quality, the instructor introduces reference performance, often human-level performance, as an aspirational benchmark that helps diagnose whether a system is underperforming [ts=3263s]. After deployment, strong train/test performance is not enough because the world can change through data drift or concept drift: seasonal clothing, scarves, sunglasses, rain, geography, and user behavior can alter the distribution or the target mapping [ts=3310s]. Simple non-ML systems can sometimes be less susceptible to drift than high-capacity learned models because they tune fewer parameters and have fewer ways to overfit a narrow distribution [ts=3601s]. Production teams should gather privacy-respecting telemetry when possible, brainstorm possible failure modes, plot many metrics initially, prune uninformative dashboards, set alarms for abnormal ranges, and maintain the model by collecting new data and updating the system [ts=3735s].

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
source_first_seen.unit_name: Sampling, conditioning, latent diffusion, and video generation
source_first_seen.unit_summary: At test time, a trained diffusion model can start from random Gaussian noise and progressively denoise it by repeatedly predicting and subtracting noise [ts=5641s]. The instructor notes that repeated diffusion calls make image generation computationally heavy, and conditioning is needed when the user wants a specific object or prompt-guided result rather than whatever the model would generate [ts=5769s]. Latent diffusion addresses cost by using an autoencoder to map images into a lower-dimensional latent space, run the noising and denoising process there, and decode back to pixels at the end [ts=5884s]. The latent representation should keep important patterns while dropping irrelevant detail, making the same diffusion idea faster and less expensive [ts=6049s]. Finally, video generation adds a temporal dimension, so the latent representation must preserve consistency across frames and can be divided into spatio-temporal patches or “cubes” used as tokens [ts=6199s].

source_first_seen.unit_name: Deep Q-learning and bootstrapped targets
source_first_seen.unit_summary: Deep Q-learning replaces a memory-heavy Q-table with a neural Q-function, using a forward pass to estimate action values from a state [ts=2136s] [ts=2161s]. For the toy example, a one-hot encoded state is fed to a network whose output layer has one Q-value per action; more actions would require more output neurons [ts=2187s] [ts=2216s]. The training target is bootstrapped from immediate reward plus discounted maximum Q-value at the next state, while that target is held fixed for the current backpropagation step [ts=2476s] [ts=2524s]. The vanilla DQN loop initializes the Q-network, loops through episodes and time steps, selects the action with maximum Q-value, observes reward and next state, computes the target/loss, and updates parameters with gradient descent [ts=3107s] [ts=3163s].

target_first_seen.unit_summary: The training section revisits DQN implementation and highlights that terminal states must be handled specially because there is no next-state future reward after the episode ends [ts=3670s] [ts=3714s]. source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
source_first_seen.unit_name: Why diffusion and how forward noising works
source_first_seen.unit_summary: Diffusion is motivated by two GAN limitations: mode collapse, where G covers only a narrow subset of outputs, and instability from training two coupled models simultaneously [ts=4597s]. The instructor uses diffusion-versus-GAN examples to argue that diffusion can produce more variety and better coverage of a real distribution, such as single and grouped flamingos or more varied burgers [ts=4650s]. A diffusion model avoids the minimax game by training one model on a denoising task designed to model the entire data distribution with more stable gradients [ts=4714s]. The forward diffusion process starts from a clean image x0 and progressively adds Gaussian noise until the picture is no longer recognizable [ts=4880s]. In the simplified recurrence, x_{t+1} is x_t plus Gaussian noise, and x_t can be viewed as x0 plus cumulative noise that must later be predicted [ts=4932s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
target_first_seen.unit_name: Diffusion denoising objective and self-supervised training set
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The reverse process trains a diffusion model to predict the cumulative noise epsilon-hat that was added between x0 and a noisy image xt [ts=5064s]. If the predicted noise can be subtracted from xt, the model can recover the original clean image, so denoising becomes the core generative skill [ts=5097s]. The reconstruction loss compares the true stored noise with the model’s predicted cumulative noise, and this is self-supervised because the forward process created the labels [ts=5161s]. The training database is built from noisy images, a time-step index t, and the cumulative noise epsilon; the index tells the model how much denoising is being requested [ts=5232s]. Before inference, the instructor summarizes the training loop as sampling triplets, computing reconstruction loss, and using gradients to teach the model to predict noise given a noisy picture [ts=5435s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
target_first_seen.unit_name: Why diffusion and how forward noising works
target_first_seen.unit_summary: Diffusion is motivated by two GAN limitations: mode collapse, where G covers only a narrow subset of outputs, and instability from training two coupled models simultaneously [ts=4597s]. The instructor uses diffusion-versus-GAN examples to argue that diffusion can produce more variety and better coverage of a real distribution, such as single and grouped flamingos or more varied burgers [ts=4650s]. A diffusion model avoids the minimax game by training one model on a denoising task designed to model the entire data distribution with more stable gradients [ts=4714s]. The forward diffusion process starts from a clean image x0 and progressively adds Gaussian noise until the picture is no longer recognizable [ts=4880s]. In the simplified recurrence, x_{t+1} is x_t plus Gaussian noise, and x_t can be viewed as x0 plus cumulative noise that must later be predicted [ts=4932s].

target_first_seen.unit_summary: GANs are introduced as a two-model adversarial training method: the generator is the model ultimately used, while the discriminator is used to train it [ts=3373s]. In the checkpoint case study, the instructor asks what evidence to inspect when reasoning benchmarks regress, safety evals fail, and tool-use latency spikes [ts=157s]. target_first_seen.unit_name: GPT-3, in-context learning, scaling laws, and prompting
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The final segment centers on GPT-3, a much larger decoder-only model that could sometimes perform new tasks without parameter updates, simply from examples placed in the prompt [ts=3995s] [ts=4052s]. This behavior is named in-context learning: the model infers a pattern from demonstrations in the current input—translation, addition, typo correction—and continues it without explicit fine-tuning [ts=4052s] [ts=4102s]. The lecture stresses that the mechanism is still poorly understood: some behavior may come from matching patterns seen during pretraining, while some appears to reflect nontrivial adaptation to the presented context [ts=4141s] [ts=4230s]. The recap defines a model as architecture plus trained parameters, using a cat classifier to separate the blueprint from the numerical weights [ts=234s]. Learning is described as repeated comparison of prediction to ground truth through a loss function, followed by gradient updates that calibrate parameters over batches of data [ts=303s]. The instructor also previews design axes that can change across projects: input modality, output type, architecture, loss, activations, optimizer, and hyperparameters [ts=375s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 2: Supervised, Self-Supervised, and Weakly Supervised Learning
target_first_seen.unit_name: Neurons, multi-class labels, capacity, and embeddings
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The instructor connects a neuron to logistic regression: flatten image pixels, apply W transpose X plus B, then pass through sigmoid to obtain a probability [ts=536s]. For multiple animals, the output layer and labels both need to change; forgetting to change labels after changing the data is described as a common project mistake [ts=662s]. One-hot vectors represent a single true class, while multi-hot vectors allow multiple labels in the same image [ts=722s]. Deeper networks have more capacity, which can be necessary for complex data but can also overfit if capacity exceeds dataset complexity [ts=813s]. The face-network example shows early layers encoding edges, middle layers encoding parts like eyes or noses, and deeper layers encoding higher-level facial features; embeddings are encodings where distance carries semantic meaning [ts=900s].

edge_labels.best_rationale: A logistic-regression neuron is the simplest supervised classifier unit, so the supervised data-driven loop is prerequisite context.

The pre-deep-learning era emphasized parts, edges, grouping, matching, and handcrafted representations, with limited success on full recognition.

source_first_seen.unit_name: Roadmap, scale, and the deep learning resurgence
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The instructor frames the lecture as a short review of extra neural-net concepts before moving into language models and then recurrent neural networks, with transformers deferred to later lectures [ts=9s] [ts=56s]. He motivates the topic by noting that modern language models are enormous deep systems, then reviews how backprop enabled hidden-layer neural nets in the 1980s and 1990s but deeper networks were long believed too hard to train until late-2000s and 2010s ideas reversed that stagnation [ts=177s] [ts=354s] [ts=422s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Neuroscience and early computer vision foundations
target_first_seen.unit_summary: This segment begins with Hubel and Wiesel's 1959 experiments on mammalian vision, emphasizing two principles: neurons in early visual cortex have local receptive fields and respond to simple oriented patterns, and visual processing is hierarchical, with increasingly complex features built from simpler ones [ts=485s] [ts=600s]. Li explicitly notes that this perspective profoundly influenced neural network modeling for vision [ts=623s]. The lecture then introduces Larry Roberts' 1963 work on shape as an early PhD thesis in computer vision and places it alongside the optimistic 1966 MIT summer vision project as landmarks in the field's origin [ts=666s] [ts=769s]. David Marr's 1970s framework is presented as a staged pipeline from input image to primal sketch, 2.5D sketch, and ultimately 3D representation [ts=773s] [ts=847s]. Li pauses to explain that recovering 3D structure from 2D measurements is fundamentally ill-posed, which is why nature uses multiple eyes and correspondence, yet even humans do not recover perfect geometry [ts=880s] [ts=958s]. She contrasts vision with language by arguing that language is generated and sequential, while vision must model a real physical world governed by physics and materials [ts=968s] [ts=1018s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: Classical hand-crafted features historically precede the deep-learning resurgence; the resurgence is not prerequisite to understand classical CV features.
edge_labels.best_rationale: Classical hand-crafted features historically precede the deep-learning resurgence; the resurgence is not prerequisite to understand classical CV features.

p5_trace.keep_rationale: Kept because deep learning resurgence from data, compute, and scale is treated as prerequisite machinery before classical computer vision and hand-crafted features becomes the main idea in one unit, though the dependency is evidenced only once.

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
source_first_seen.unit_name: Diffusion denoising objective and self-supervised training set
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The reverse process trains a diffusion model to predict the cumulative noise epsilon-hat that was added between x0 and a noisy image xt [ts=5064s]. If the predicted noise can be subtracted from xt, the model can recover the original clean image, so denoising becomes the core generative skill [ts=5097s]. The reconstruction loss compares the true stored noise with the model’s predicted cumulative noise, and this is self-supervised because the forward process created the labels [ts=5161s]. The training database is built from noisy images, a time-step index t, and the cumulative noise epsilon; the index tells the model how much denoising is being requested [ts=5232s]. Before inference, the instructor summarizes the training loop as sampling triplets, computing reconstruction loss, and using gradients to teach the model to predict noise given a noisy picture [ts=5435s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
target_first_seen.unit_name: Sampling, conditioning, latent diffusion, and video generation
target_first_seen.unit_summary: At test time, a trained diffusion model can start from random Gaussian noise and progressively denoise it by repeatedly predicting and subtracting noise [ts=5641s]. The instructor notes that repeated diffusion calls make image generation computationally heavy, and conditioning is needed when the user wants a specific object or prompt-guided result rather than whatever the model would generate [ts=5769s]. Latent diffusion addresses cost by using an autoencoder to map images into a lower-dimensional latent space, run the noising and denoising process there, and decode back to pixels at the end [ts=5884s]. The latent representation should keep important patterns while dropping irrelevant detail, making the same diffusion idea faster and less expensive [ts=6049s]. Finally, video generation adds a temporal dimension, so the latent representation must preserve consistency across frames and can be divided into spatio-temporal patches or “cubes” used as tokens [ts=6199s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: Sampling and conditioning apply the denoising intuition at inference time.
edge_labels.best_rationale: Sampling and conditioning apply the denoising intuition at inference time.

p5_trace.keep_rationale: Sampling and conditioning use the learned denoising model after diffusion training.

target_first_seen.unit_name: Generalized diffusion perspectives and autoregressive latents
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The final technical segment broadens from rectified flow to a generalized diffusion design space [ts=3841s]. Rectified flow is restated as sampling x, z, and t, setting xt as a linear interpolation, setting the ground-truth velocity vgt=z-x, predicting v from f_theta(xt,t), and minimizing an L2 loss [ts=3864s], [ts=3894s]. Other diffusion formulations vary the t distribution, the functions used to mix x and z into xt, and the target ygt that the network predicts [ts=3916s], [ts=3946s]. Examples include variance-preserving schedules, variance-exploding schedules, x-prediction, noise-prediction, and v-prediction [ts=3990s], [ts=4026s]. The lecturer then names three mathematical perspectives without deriving them: diffusion as a latent variable model similar to a VAE optimizing a variational lower bound [ts=4074s], diffusion as score-function learning where the score is the gradient of log pdata(x) pointing toward high-density regions [ts=4117s], and diffusion as solving stochastic differential equations with learned numerical integrators [ts=4176s]. The lecture closes by noting that autoregressive models also return in modern pipelines when trained over discrete latents from an encoder-decoder, so GANs, VAEs, autoregressive models, and diffusion all combine in contemporary generative systems [ts=4265s], [ts=4298s].

edge_labels.best_rationale: Mathematical views of diffusion build on the basic denoising/noise-removal intuition.

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
source_first_seen.unit_name: The GAN generator-discriminator game
source_first_seen.unit_summary: GANs are introduced as a two-model adversarial training method: the generator is the model ultimately used, while the discriminator is used to train it [ts=3373s]. The generator maps a small random code z into a larger image, so its architecture must upsample from a low-dimensional input to a high-dimensional output [ts=3406s]. The discriminator alternates between generated images and real database images and learns binary labels, predicting fake as 0 and real as 1 [ts=3511s]. Training succeeds when the generator becomes realistic enough that a strong discriminator can no longer reliably distinguish real from fake [ts=3562s]. Gradients flow through the discriminator and back into the generator, making the simultaneous optimization of two networks a stability challenge [ts=3586s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 4: Adversarial Robustness and Generative Models
target_first_seen.unit_name: GAN objectives, training problems, and code-space structure
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The discriminator loss is framed as binary cross-entropy with one term for correctly labeling real images as 1 and another for labeling generated images as 0 [ts=3817s]. The generator objective is the opposite side of the game: it tries to make the discriminator’s judgment bad, but the original minimax cost creates a cold-start issue when generated images are obviously fake [ts=3939s]. Because D(G(z)) is near 0 early in training, the saturating generator cost is flat and gives tiny gradients; the non-saturating cost is introduced to give the generator a stronger early learning signal [ts=4063s]. The instructor then describes mode collapse, where the generator fools the discriminator with a narrow subset of outputs rather than learning the full data distribution [ts=4289s]. Alternating training schedules and code-space arithmetic, such as moving from “man with glasses” minus “man” plus “woman” toward “woman with glasses,” illustrate practical GAN behavior and latent structure [ts=4339s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: GAN instability diagnostics follow from the adversarial minimax training dynamics.
edge_labels.best_rationale: GAN instability diagnostics follow from the adversarial minimax training dynamics.

p5_trace.keep_rationale: GAN instability and mode collapse are diagnosed through the GAN objective/training dynamics.

source_first_seen.unit_name: GPT-3, in-context learning, scaling laws, and prompting
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The final segment centers on GPT-3, a much larger decoder-only model that could sometimes perform new tasks without parameter updates, simply from examples placed in the prompt [ts=3995s] [ts=4052s]. This behavior is named in-context learning: the model infers a pattern from demonstrations in the current input—translation, addition, typo correction—and continues it without explicit fine-tuning [ts=4052s] [ts=4102s]. The lecture stresses that the mechanism is still poorly understood: some behavior may come from matching patterns seen during pretraining, while some appears to reflect nontrivial adaptation to the presented context [ts=4141s] [ts=4230s]. It then turns to scaling, noting that larger models trained on more data generally improved, but that compute must be allocated wisely; Chinchilla is cited as evidence that GPT-3 was over-parameterized relative to the amount of training data and that smaller models trained on more tokens can do better [ts=4234s] [ts=4290s]. Finally, the segment introduces chain-of-thought prompting as giving worked intermediate steps in the prompt, which often improves reasoning by letting the model generate a scratchpad, while also emphasizing open concerns about emergent behavior, bias, programming use, and continued domain-adaptive pretraining such as the "Don't Stop Pretraining" idea [ts=4310s] [ts=4634s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Flamingo training, few-shot behavior, and benchmark shift
target_first_seen.unit_summary: Flamingo’s training uses long interleaved image-text sequences rather than isolated image-caption pairs [ts=2131s]. A masking scheme ensures that when generating the description for a particular image, the model attends only to that image’s visual features, even though it sees a longer context of images and descriptions [ts=2184s]. This supports applications such as multi-turn dialogue about an image, where a user can ask follow-up questions and the model inherits reasoning capabilities from the underlying language model [ts=2233s] [ts=2257s]. It also supports multi-image reasoning and in-context learning: users can provide examples of image-caption or image-question-answer pairs and ask the model to continue the pattern on a new image [ts=2306s] [ts=2320s]. The lecturer clarifies that giving examples is few-shot learning, while removing those examples would make the task zero-shot [ts=2397s]. Flamingo’s results helped shift the field from reporting mostly classification benchmarks to reporting any visual understanding task that can be framed as question answering [ts=2450s] [ts=2471s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: Multimodal few-shot reasoning extends in-context learning to image-text demonstrations and prompts.
edge_labels.best_rationale: Multimodal few-shot reasoning extends in-context learning to image-text demonstrations and prompts.

p5_trace.keep_rationale: CS230 zero/few-shot prompting provides language-model context for multimodal few-shot reasoning.

target_first_seen.unit_name: Text-to-video diffusion and distillation
target_first_seen.unit_summary: Text-to-video diffusion keeps the same broad latent diffusion pipeline as text-to-image, but the latent tensor gains a temporal dimension in addition to height and width [ts=3530s], [ts=3544s]. The decoder becomes a spatial-temporal autoencoder that upsamples latents into video pixels [ts=3555s]. The major bottleneck is sequence length: high-resolution, high-FPS, many-frame video produces far more tokens than images [ts=3580s]. The lecture contrasts roughly 1,024 image tokens in a state-of-the-art text-to-image model with about 76,000 video tokens in the discussed text-to-video example [ts=3592s], [ts=3609s]. It frames 2024-2025 as a rapid era of video diffusion models, with Sora cited as an influential scaling moment for video diffusion transformers [ts=3623s], [ts=3661s]. The instructor also mentions very recent video generation examples that jointly model audio with video [ts=3703s], [ts=3730s]. The segment ends with diffusion distillation: because sampling may require 30-50 or more model evaluations, distillation attempts to reduce inference steps while preserving sample quality, sometimes even reaching single-step sampling at a quality cost [ts=3750s], [ts=3783s].

edge_labels.source_description: A way to categorize generation tasks by how many valid outputs they permit, with entropy used as a formal intuition for openness. Open-ended tasks have many valid answers and graded quality, so evaluation must move beyond exact labels.
edge_labels.target_description: Training a model to predict the next token from its prefix, used directly for decoder pretraining and as a baseline pretraining objective more broadly. Autoregressive models make sequence modeling tractable by factoring p(x) into conditional next-part distributions over an ordered decomposition of x.

source_first_seen.unit_name: What NLG is and how tasks vary by open-endedness
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The segment defines natural language generation as NLP where the output is natural language, contrasting it with understanding tasks whose input is language [ts=155s]. It notes a historical shift from rule-based templates and infilling to deep learning systems [ts=189s]. The lecture then surveys examples including machine translation, digital assistants, summarization, creative story writing, data-to-text, image captioning, and ChatGPT as a general-purpose NLG system [ts=214s] [ts=280s]. It organizes tasks by open-endedness: translation and summarization have relatively constrained output spaces, dialogue allows multiple valid continuations, and story generation has extremely large valid output space [ts=348s] [ts=432s]. The segment closes by formalizing this spectrum with entropy, arguing that high-entropy tasks are more open-ended and that this distinction will matter for both decoding and training choices [ts=493s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Language models and n-gram fundamentals
target_first_seen.unit_summary: A language model is defined as a system that assigns a probability distribution to the next token given the previous context, and equivalently as a model that assigns probability to an entire sequence via a chain-rule decomposition into next-token conditionals [ts=1714s] [ts=1777s] [ts=1821s]. The lecture stresses that language models long predate ChatGPT and underlie autocomplete and query suggestion systems [ts=1862s] [ts=1882s] [ts=1928s]. It then introduces n-gram language models, where a Markov assumption keeps only the most recent n-1 words and predicts the next word from relative frequencies of observed short contexts [ts=1975s] [ts=2106s] [ts=2157s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: Autoregressive language modeling is a foundational generation mechanism; open-ended generation/evaluation is not prerequisite machinery for next-token modeling.

source_first_seen.unit_name: Limitations of supervised fine-tuning
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The instructor summarizes instruction fine-tuning as simple, then lists why it is not enough [ts=2043s] [ts=2068s]. It depends on expensive human demonstrations, especially for specialized questions that may require high expertise [ts=2076s] [ts=2098s]. Many open-ended or creative tasks do not have a single correct answer [ts=2116s] [ts=2125s]. Token-level language modeling loss also treats mistakes too uniformly: calling Avatar an adventure show and calling it a musical can be penalized similarly despite very different semantic severity [ts=2135s] [ts=2164s]. Another issue is that human-written answers may become a bottleneck as models generate better answers than labelers [ts=2169s] [ts=2192s]. The main conceptual problem is objective mismatch: the desired goal is outputs humans prefer, but SFT still performs next-token prediction on curated data [ts=2215s] [ts=2238s].

target_first_seen.unit_name: Exposure bias, alternative training schemes, and RLHF context
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The lecture revisits repetition from the training side and argues that maximum-likelihood language models can assign high probability to bad degenerate strings [ts=2473s]. The core diagnosis is exposure bias: under teacher forcing the model trains on gold prefixes, but at generation time it must condition on its own imperfect outputs, creating a harmful train-test mismatch [ts=2510s] [ts=2541s]. Scheduled sampling narrows this gap by mixing model-generated and gold tokens with a probability that increases through training, though the objective can be unstable [ts=2560s]. DAgger similarly augments training data with model-generated sequences so the model learns on states it will actually encounter [ts=2603s]. The lecture also presents retrieval-augmented generation, where the model begins from a retrieved prototype and edits it by insertion, deletion, or swapping, reducing exposure bias because generation no longer starts from scratch left-to-right [ts=2655s]. Reinforcement learning is then framed as an MDP over states, actions, policies, and rewards, with rewards derived from automatic metrics or human preference [ts=2693s] [ts=2827s]. The lecture warns that optimizing BLEU or ROUGE can game the metric rather than improve true quality [ts=2744s]. It finishes with the modern pipeline behind ChatGPT-style systems: large-scale pretraining, instruction tuning, and then RLHF, with RLHF viewed as difficult from scratch but effective on top of a strong pretrained model [ts=3110s] [ts=3130s].

edge_labels.baseline_gpt54_rationale: Detailed RLHF preference optimization is more specific than the general NLG/RLHF concept; the dependency direction is not source-before-target.
edge_labels.best_rationale: Detailed RLHF preference optimization is more specific than the general NLG/RLHF concept; the dependency direction is not source-before-target.

p5_trace.keep_rationale: RLHF over text generation uses reward models trained from human preference comparisons.

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lec. 19 - Model Interpretability & Editing, Been Kim
target_first_seen.unit_name: Attribution methods, hypothesis testing, and the limits of saliency maps
target_first_seen.unit_summary: The lecture first defines a saliency map as a feature-wise estimate of how prediction changes locally around an input, using ImageNet pixels as the intuitive example [ts=602s] [ts=623s]. Kim then gives several reasons a gap can arise between what machines know and what humans think they know, and drills into attribution methods by showing that trained and untrained networks can produce nearly identical saliency maps, while inserted bugs such as label noise, spurious correlations, or OOD shifts are not reliably surfaced by explanations [ts=671s] [ts=743s] [ts=789s]. She reformulates the user’s interpretation problem as hypothesis testing and argues that IG and SHAP cannot validate such hypotheses better than random in theory and around random in practical end tasks like recourse and spurious-correlation detection [ts=935s] [ts=965s] [ts=1074s]. Her practical replacement is simple local sampling around the point of interest, with usefulness governed by sample count, output resolution, and feature count, plus careful validation before deploying these methods in high-stakes settings [ts=1115s] [ts=1147s] [ts=1240s].

source_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 2: Supervised, Self-Supervised, and Weakly Supervised Learning
source_first_seen.unit_name: Self-supervised image embeddings and contrastive learning
source_first_seen.unit_summary: The self-supervised section begins from the cost of labels and asks how to learn face or image embeddings from unlabeled images in the wild [ts=4853s]. The instructor contrasts older supervised triplets with an augmentation-based method: rotate, crop, patch, translate, or otherwise perturb the same image and train the network to map both views to nearby vectors [ts=5037s]. This creates labels from the data itself, because the pair identity is generated by the augmentation pipeline rather than by human annotation [ts=5100s]. SimCLR is presented as an example of this contrastive self-supervised approach, shifting from supervised triplets like FaceNet to self-supervised pairs [ts=5148s]. The reason this matters is scale: scripts can create augmented pairs from massive unlabeled datasets, leaving compute as a major bottleneck [ts=5164s].

target_first_seen.lecture_title: Lecture 16 - Multimodal Deep Learning, Douwe Kiela
target_first_seen.unit_name: From CLIP to multimodal transformers and FLAVA
target_first_seen.unit_summary: Late fusion is reframed as modern contrastive learning, with CLIP as the canonical example: independently encode text and images, use in-batch negatives, and rank matched pairs above mismatched ones [ts=1402s][ts=1441s]. Kiela emphasizes that CLIP’s leap came less from a novel loss than from transformer encoders and massive web-scale paired data, enabling prompt-based zero-shot classification and robust transfer; ALIGN and LAION continue the same scaling story with more data [ts=1503s][ts=1561s][ts=1667s]. He then walks through BERT-era multimodal transformers such as VisualBERT, ViLBERT, MMBT, PixelBERT, UNITER, and ViLT, contrasting single-stream versus dual-stream fusion and showing the trend from detector features toward raw patch-based transformer inputs [ts=1828s][ts=1869s][ts=2021s][ts=2061s]. The segment culminates in FLAVA, a “one model to rule them all” design that jointly pretrains image-only, text-only, and multimodal objectives, combining masked image modeling, masked language modeling, image-text matching, and a global contrastive loss in one shared foundation model [ts=2207s][ts=2331s][ts=2399s].
